cur:catacombs-adelphia-sarcophagus.summary: A shell with the portraits of Adelphia and her husband divides two registers crowded with scenes: Christ heals the woman with the issue of blood and the blind man, multiplies the loaves, raises the widow's son, changes water into wine at Cana and enters Jerusalem, while the Magi adore the Child. It is the masterpiece of Christian sculpture in Sicily.
facts: It was found in 1872 in the Rotunda of Adelphia in the Catacombs of San Giovanni, Syracuse.
The lid inscription reads 'Here lies Adelfia, clarissima femina, wife of Count Valerius'.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: In a band across the foot of the page, the haloed Christ sits within a green medallion holding a book, flanked by two flying angels, while two great winged cherubim appear below him. The image illustrates the verse 'he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: he flew upon the wings of the wind' (Vulgate Psalm 17:11).
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:objects-berlin-relief-panel-baptism-.summary: Three scenes are stacked on this narrow ivory leaf: at the top Herod, enthroned, orders the Massacre of the Innocents; in the middle John the Baptist lays his hand on the head of the small, naked Christ standing in the stream of the Jordan; and at the bottom the haloed Christ touches with his staff the water jars at the wedding at Cana as a servant pours. The panel moves from the threat to the infant Christ to his manifestation at the Jordan and his first sign at Cana.
facts: The museum attributes the panel to Rome or Milan in the first half of the 5th century; it probably formed part of a five-part book cover or diptych (type).
In Early Christian art Christ often performs miracles with a staff or wand, as here at Cana (type).
